query_text: Should we rely on self-driving cars for transportation?

action.query: NHTSA automated vehicles safety self driving cars 2025
queries: NHTSA automated vehicles safety self driving cars 2025
IIHS autonomous vehicles safety study self driving cars

annotations.title: Despite warnings, many people treat partially automated vehicles as self-driving
Standing General Order on Crash Reporting | NHTSA

content.text:
**Short answer: not as a blanket replacement yet.** We should rely on self-driving cars **selectively**—in places and conditions where they have been extensively tested and regulated—but we should **not yet assume they are safe, available, or suitable for all transportation needs.**

A good middle-ground view is:

- **Yes, for limited robotaxi services** in mapped, supported areas, especially if the provider has strong safety data, remote support, clear operating limits, and public oversight.
- **No, for general “my car drives itself anywhere” use.** NHTSA still distinguishes today’s limited automated-driving deployments from a broadly available self-driving car you can buy and use everywhere. ([nhtsa.gov](https://www.nhtsa.gov/vehicle-safety/automated-vehicles-safety?utm_source=openai))
- **Be especially cautious with “partial automation.”** Systems marketed as driver-assistance can encourage people to over-trust them; IIHS has found many users treat partially automated vehicles as if they were fully self-driving, even though they still require supervision. ([iihs.org](https://www.iihs.org/news/detail/despite-warnings-many-people-treat-partially-automated-vehicles-as-self-driving?utm_source=openai))

The strongest argument **for** self-driving cars is that human driving is dangerous, and well-designed automated systems do not get drunk, distracted, sleepy, or angry. Waymo, for example, reports safety analyses suggesting its driverless service reduces injury and fatality risk in the areas where it operates. ([waymo.com](https://waymo.com/safetyreport/?utm_source=openai))

The strongest argument **against relying on them too much too soon** is that the technology still has edge cases: unusual road situations, emergency vehicles, school buses, construction zones, poor weather, unclear human behavior, and software failures. Regulators are still updating rules and collecting crash reports, which suggests the system is not mature enough for universal reliance. ([nhtsa.gov](https://www.nhtsa.gov/node/103486?utm_source=openai))

So my recommendation would be:

**Use self-driving cars as one option in the transportation mix, not as the foundation of transportation policy yet.** They can be useful for ride-hailing, accessibility, late-night trips, airport transfers, and reducing some crash risks—but cities and individuals should still invest in public transit, walkability, cycling infrastructure, conventional taxis, and human-driven vehicles until autonomous systems prove safe across many more environments.
